system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2151-01-28 16:01:00 to 2151-02-03 13:22:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis presented with left arm pain due to worsening steal syndrome in his left brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula. He underwent elective fistula banding the following day, which was successful in reducing blood flow to alleviate symptoms while preserving access function. He remained asymptomatic postoperatively with no neurovascular deficits. His potassium was elevated at 6.4 on admission but decreased after an extended hemodialysis session. He tolerated a regular diet, maintained baseline functional status, and was discharged in stable condition to an extended care facility. Follow-up was arranged with transplant surgery and sleep medicine. Home medications were resumed, and discharge instructions included monitoring for arm symptoms, weight changes, and dialysis access issues.
problems: Other complications due to renal dialysis device, implant, and graft
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ year old man s/p banding on ___ of LUE AV fistula still
with significant steal while on dialysis. // Please assess arterial
vasculature flow in patients left arm, has LUE brachiocephalic arteriovenous
fistula.

COMPARISON:  Av fistulogram performed ___

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow) and Dr.
___ radiology attending) performed the procedure. The
attending, Dr. ___ was present and supervising throughout the procedure.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
75 mcg of fentanyl throughout the total intra-service time of 75 min during
which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored by an
independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine was injected in the skin and
subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: Fentanyl
CONTRAST: 155 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 19 min 6 sec, 54 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1. Left subclavian arteriogram.
2. Left brachial arteriogram.
3. Left radial arteriogram
4. Left ulnar arteriogram.
5. Left brachial and radial arteriogram with compression of fistula.
6. Left brachial arteriogram after intra-arterial nitroglycerin.
PROCEDURE DETAILS:
Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and alternatives to the
procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the patient. The patient
was then brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the exam table.
The left upper extremity and right groin were prepped and draped in the usual
sterile fashion.  A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___ protocol.
 Using palpatory and fluoroscopic guidance, the right common femoral artery
was punctured using a micropuncture set at the level of the mid-femoral head.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having some trouble with your left hand during dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. My hand gets so cold and hurts bad every time I go for dialysis. I can't even finish the session sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you’ve been wearing a glove on your left hand?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's always cold. Feels like it's never warm, even inside.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. This could be related to your AV fistula and something called steal syndrome. We saw your blood pressure was low in clinic—around 90s systolic—but you didn’t feel dizzy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t feel lightheaded or anything. Just weak sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’re going to hold off on your diltiazem and isosorbide for now. They might be lowering your blood pressure too much, which could worsen the blood flow to your hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So those meds are making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll restart a lower dose once we stabilize things. Cardiology is reviewing your case to help manage your heart and blood pressure safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to do an arteriogram today to look at the blood flow in your left arm. It’s a special X-ray with contrast to see how blood moves through your arteries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some numbing medicine and light sedation. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. We need to see if there’s a blockage or why the blood isn’t reaching your hand well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the results back from your arteriogram. Good news—no major blockages in the big arteries like the subclavian or brachial.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the cold and pain then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw poor filling in the smaller arteries—the radial and ulnar—down in your forearm. Even when we temporarily blocked the fistula and gave medicine to open the vessels, the flow didn’t improve much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the banding didn’t fix it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helped some, but not enough. The issue seems to be in the small vessels themselves. We don’t see a structural blockage, so it might be a circulation problem we can manage with medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting your diltiazem at a lower dose—120 mg once daily. We’re also adding two new medications: digoxin and midodrine, which we’ll give before dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do those do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Digoxin helps your heart pump more efficiently. Midodrine helps raise your blood pressure during dialysis, so more blood can reach your hand and reduce steal symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I feel different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so—less pain and coldness during dialysis. We’ll monitor your blood pressure closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned shoulder pain from a fall a few weeks ago. We’re going to get an X-ray of your left arm to check for any injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t think it was broken. Just hurts when I move it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows a healing fracture in the middle of your left humerus. It’s not displaced and is healing on its own. Ortho says no surgery needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fracture? I didn’t know that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely from your fall. It’s stable and not near the joint, so it should heal with time. This might be contributing to your arm pain, separate from the fistula issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the pain isn’t all from the dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. The fracture explains the shoulder and upper arm pain. The coldness and pain during dialysis are still from the steal syndrome, but we’re treating that differently now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did dialysis go this morning? Any pain or coldness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I didn’t have to stop early. The pain was less, and my hand wasn’t as cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The midodrine and digoxin seem to be helping. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need to take these meds forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with digoxin every other day and midodrine before each dialysis. We need to check your digoxin level in a few days to make sure it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only if the level gets too high. We’ll monitor it closely. The goal is 0.6 to 1.2. As long as it’s in range, it’s safe and helps your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today to an extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not completely, but we’ve improved things. Your hand pain during dialysis is better, and your blood pressure is more stable. The fracture will heal on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor if your left hand gets colder, more painful, turns blue, or you lose grip strength. Also check your fistula daily for the buzzing sound and pulse—called bruit and thrill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I don’t feel it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call right away. That could mean the fistula is clotting. Don’t wait for your dialysis day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue most as before. Diltiazem is now 120 mg daily, digoxin every other day, and midodrine before dialysis. Keep taking your insulin, gabapentin, and other usual meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—low sodium, low potassium, low phosphorus. Follow your nephrologist’s fluid limits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your records go to the facility. Keep up with your dialysis and follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take care, and call if anything changes with your hand or fistula.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nephrologist will follow up. We’ll coordinate care. Just focus on healing and staying on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're doing great. We’ll get you discharged shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—keep wearing that glove if it helps. It’s okay to protect your hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Feels better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. We’re making progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re a team. You’re doing your part—staying engaged and asking questions. That helps us help you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you will. We’ve got a plan, and you’re responding well. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Rest up, and the care team will get you ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be in touch if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A man with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis was admitted due to persistent steal syndrome symptoms in his left hand despite prior fistula banding. He reported chronic coldness and severe pain during dialysis, requiring early session termination. Hypotension was noted, prompting temporary hold of diltiazem and isosorbide. After cardiology consultation, he was restarted on a lower dose of diltiazem and initiated on digoxin and midodrine before dialysis, which improved blood pressure and reduced steal symptoms. An arteriogram showed no major arterial blockages but persistent poor distal radial and ulnar artery filling, even after fistula compression and nitroglycerin. A healing, non-displaced mid-humerus fracture was incidentally found on X-ray, contributing to shoulder pain. He responded well to treatment, completed dialysis without pain, and was discharged to an extended care facility with medication adjustments, fistula monitoring instructions, and plans for digoxin level checks.
